Consult Summary:
- Known asthmatic with hay fever presenting with 2–3 days of exertional shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough with minimal relief from salbutamol; impression is a mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation with possible exercise-induced contribution.

History:
- Presenting complaint/timeline: New onset (2–3 days) shortness of breath noted first while running; currently occurs with brisk walking. Wheeze and cough present. Blue (salbutamol) inhaler offers little/no relief.
- Associated symptoms: Wheeze, cough. Denies sputum production.
- Pertinent negatives: No prior asthma hospitalizations. No prior oral steroids. No known drug allergies.
- Past medical history: Asthma. Hay fever. Possible eczema (patient uses emollient and topical hydrocortisone; not clearly confirmed).
- Family history: Brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Medications: Salbutamol (blue) PRN and used prophylactically; patient reports using a preventer inhaler twice daily (name not clearly stated). Topicals: cetraben and hydrocortisone. Initial mention of “Bactroban” retracted/clarified.
- Prior control: Last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; last asthma review ~2 years ago.
- Social/preventive: Physically active (running). Smoking status not discussed.

Examination:
- No in-person exam/vitals obtained (telehealth).
- No current peak flow performed. Baseline (“when well”) peak flow approximately 380 L/min by recall.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation on background of persistent asthma.
  - Evidence: 2–3 days of wheeze, cough, exertional dyspnea; frequent reliever use with poor relief; atopic history; previously controlled asthma now deteriorated.
- Additional considerations (ranked):
  1) Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction contributing (onset with running; persists with brisk walking).
  2) Poor inhaler technique or suboptimal controller regimen contributing to loss of control (confusion about medications; poor response to SABA; last review 2 years ago).
  3) Allergic trigger possible (hay fever; atopic history), though no acute allergy symptoms documented.

Plan:
- Medications:
  - Increase brown preventer (Clenil per clinician) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review.
  - Use salbutamol (blue) as needed up to every 2–4 hours; frequent need indicates poor control.
- Follow-up:
  - Book face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for chest examination and peak flow measurement.
  - Depending on findings, may require oral steroids and/or antibiotics (to be determined at visit).
- Safety-net:
  - If breathing worsens, or if needing blue inhaler very frequently, attend A&E without waiting for the appointment.
- Additional recommendations (consistent with DDx and context):
  - At the visit: review inhaler technique and adherence; assess likely triggers (exercise, allergens).

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Smoking status; current objective measures (vitals, SpO2, peak flow); exact preventer inhaler name/strength and dosing prior to change; detailed trigger review; recent infection symptoms or contacts; pregnancy status (if relevant); personalized asthma action plan; vaccination status.  
● Conflicts noted: Medication list initially included “Flanel/Bactroban,” later clarified to cetraben and hydrocortisone; eczema history suggested by clinician but not clearly confirmed by patient; reliever frequency guidance stated as “every 2–4 hours,” later also “up to every two hourly.”  
● Transcript quality: Some incomplete/unclear segments and medication naming confusion; lacks objective data due to telehealth setting.
